    • Rule to remember: no Fourier shortcut for random patterns, so solve the x-update with CG using a matvec built from Afun, Atfun (and opDx, opDtx).
    • Ã is fixed; b̃ changes every iteration. Warm-starting CG from the previous x is an optional speedup.
    • Priors dramatically beat least norm at every compression factor; the DnCNN prior with ADMM holds up best as compression grows.
    • Next: the same machinery for LiDAR (§27).
    Part 7 · LiDAR
    27

    Compressive and Single-Pixel LiDAR

    LiDAR (light detection and ranging; Week 4 and Week 5 §20.2) measures distance by timing laser light's round trip: distance d = c t / 2, where t is the round-trip time and c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light. This week's tools matter for LiDAR in four concrete ways.

    27.1 Why LiDAR and single-pixel imaging fit together

    A depth camera needs, at every pixel, a detector fast enough to time light to within a nanosecond (a billionth of a second; light travels 30 cm in that time). Such detectors (for example single-photon avalanche diodes, SPADs, which click on individual photons) are expensive to build in large arrays, especially at the infrared wavelengths many LiDARs use (such as 1550 nm, chosen partly because it is safer for eyes). Three ways to get a depth image:

    ApproachHowDetector
    scanning LiDARsteer one laser beam across the scene, one point at a timeone fast detector
    flash LiDARlight the whole scene at oncea full array of fast detectors
    compressive (single-pixel) LiDARlight the whole scene; a DMD (§23) applies patterns; time the total returnone fast detector

    The third is §23's single-pixel camera with a timing detector. Research systems built this way have recovered depth images from fewer patterns than pixels.

    27.2 The forward model: one single-pixel problem per time bin

    Time bins. The detector does not report one time; it records a histogram: counts of returned light in each short time slot (a time bin) after the laser pulse. A bin of width Δt corresponds to a depth slice of thickness Δd = c Δt / 2.

    Worked example — bin sizes

    Δt = 1 ns gives Δd = 3 × 10⁸ × 10⁻⁹ / 2 ≈ 0.15 m per bin. Covering depths 0–30 m then takes 30 / 0.15 = 200 bins.

    The model. Describe the scene as a stack of 2D images, one per depth bin: x[p, t] is how much light pixel p sends back in time bin t (nonzero only in the bin matching that pixel's surface depth). The light reaching the detector in bin t, through pattern m, is the pattern-weighted sum of that slice:

    b[m, t] = Σ_p a_m[p] · x[p, t] ⇒ B = A X
    TermMeaningSize (64×64 scene, 4×, 200 bins)
    Athe same pattern matrix as §231024 × 4096
    Xthe scene: column t = the image of "what is at depth bin t"4096 × 200
    Bthe data: row m = the histogram recorded through pattern m1024 × 200

    Read it column by column: each time bin is an ordinary single-pixel imaging problem b_t = A x_t, all sharing the same A. HW5 Task 3's solver, run 200 times (or on all columns at once), recovers the whole depth-resolved scene.

    Worked example — 4 pixels, 2 patterns, two surfaces

    Reuse §24's scene reflectivities [0.2, 0.9, 0.4, 0.7], with pixels 1–2 on a wall in bin 3 and pixels 3–4 on a box in bin 5. Patterns a₁ = [1, 0, 1, 0], a₂ = [0, 1, 1, 1].

    bin 3 (wall)bin 5 (box)
    pattern 1 histogram0.2 (pixel 1)0.4 (pixel 3)
    pattern 2 histogram0.9 (pixel 2)0.4 + 0.7 = 1.1 (pixels 3, 4)

    Timing has already separated the two surfaces: the bin-3 column is a single-pixel measurement of the wall alone, the bin-5 column of the box alone. Adding the bins back up gives §24's readings 0.6 and 2.0 (the plain intensity image).

    A prior that fits naturally. Each depth slice x_t is mostly zero (only the pixels whose surface is at that depth are lit): the "stars" situation of §7, so an ℓ₁ prior suits each slice. Across slices, each pixel has typically one main return (sparse in time), and neighboring pixels tend to have similar depths (sparse depth gradients: TV, §27.4).

    From the cube to a depth map. For each pixel, the depth is the bin with the strongest return times 0.15 m. A cheaper variant used in practice recovers just two images with two single-pixel solves, the total reflectivity Σ_t x[p, t] and the time-weighted sum Σ_t t·x[p, t]; their ratio is each pixel's average return bin, i.e. its depth (correct when each pixel has one surface).

    The data-size picture. The full cube has 4096 × 200 = 819 200 unknowns; the data has 1024 × 200 = 204 800 numbers. The same 4× compression as HW5, with the prior making up the difference.

    One more advantage: light efficiency. Each pattern with about half its mirrors "on" sends roughly half of the whole scene's returned light to the detector, instead of one pixel's worth at a time. When the detector's own electronic noise dominates (rather than the randomness of the light itself), that larger signal per reading improves the signal-to-noise ratio. This is called the multiplex advantage.

    27.3 Counting photons changes the data term

    The problem. Long-range or low-power LiDARs often return only a handful of photons per bin. Photon arrivals are random, and their counts follow a Poisson distribution (the probability law for counting independent random events, such as raindrops landing on a tile in a minute; this is the photon shot noise of Week 2 §18), not a Gaussian: a bin expecting 4 photons gets 4 ± 2 (50% spread), while one expecting 400 gets 400 ± 20 (5%), because the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. At low counts, a Gaussian noise model is wrong: it even assigns probability to negative counts.

    §5's recipe still works; only the likelihood changes. If bin i expects (A x)_i photons, the Poisson probability of seeing b_i is (A x)_i^b_i e^{−(A x)_i} / b_i!, so

    −log p(b | x) = Σ_i [ (A x)_i − b_i log (A x)_i ] + (terms without x)
    TermMeaning
    (A x)_ithe expected photon count in measurement i if the scene were x (in practice plus a known background level from ambient light)
    b_ithe photons actually counted
    b_i!"b_i factorial," 1·2·…·b_i; it does not depend on x and drops out

    This replaces ½‖b − A x‖²/σ² as the data term. The MAP objective is still "data term + λΨ," and ADMM still applies: the data step is no longer a linear system (no closed form), but splitting can isolate it into its own simple per-measurement prox step. The deeper machinery is beyond this week; the point is that the Bayesian view tells you which data term to use when the noise is not Gaussian.

    27.4 TV for depth maps: edges stay sharp, no "flying pixels"

    Why TV fits depth even better than brightness. A depth map has no texture: a printed poster on a wall has a busy brightness image but a perfectly flat depth image. Depth maps are mostly flat or smoothly varying patches separated by sharp jumps at object boundaries: exactly what TV favors (§9).

    Flying pixels. Ordinary smoothing (averaging neighbors) at a depth edge invents depths that belong to no surface: points floating in mid-air between a foreground object and the background. These are the same artifacts LiDAR and time-of-flight users call flying pixels (or mixed pixels); a sensor also creates them on its own when one pixel's light comes partly from the foreground and partly from the background. TV's edge-preserving behavior avoids adding them.

    Worked example — a scan line across a box edge

    Measured depths, in meters, with noise: [10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.0, 15.1, 14.9, 15.0, 15.0] (a wall at 10 m, then a box surface at 15 m). Two clean-ups:

    MethodResult
    3-tap moving average (each sample averaged with its two neighbors, end values repeated)10.03, 10.00, 10.00, 11.67, 13.33, 15.00, 14.97, 15.00
    TV denoising, minimize ½‖x − b‖² + 0.2 ‖D x‖₁ (solved with this week's ADMM, ρ = 1)10.05, 10.05, 10.05, 10.05, 14.95, 14.95, 14.95, 14.95

    The average invents two flying points at 11.67 m and 13.33 m, where nothing exists. TV returns two perfectly flat plateaus and a single clean 10 → 15 m jump. Its one bias: each plateau moves toward the other by λ ÷ (plateau length) = 0.2/4 = 0.05 m, because TV charges for the jump's height (§9's "total climb") and trims it slightly. This contrast loss is TV's typical small price.

    Slanted surfaces and staircasing. A floor seen at an angle has depth that rises steadily, a constant nonzero depth gradient. Plain TV penalizes every step of that slope and may turn the ramp into flat terraces (staircasing, §9). Higher-order priors such as total generalized variation (TGV, slide 46), which penalize changes in the gradient rather than the gradient itself, treat a plane as free and fit depth maps of slanted surfaces better.

    Same concept, different names

    Single-pixel LiDAR = compressive LiDAR = compressive depth imaging. Time bin = histogram bin = range bin. Flying pixels = mixed pixels = edge artifacts in depth maps. Multiplex advantage = Fellgett advantage (the spectroscopy name).

    Summary
    • Compressive LiDAR = single-pixel camera + timing detector: B = A X, one single-pixel problem per time bin (bin depth = cΔt/2, 0.15 m for 1 ns), all sharing the same A.
    • Each depth slice is sparse (ℓ₁ prior); each pixel has one main return; depth = strongest bin × bin depth.
    • Photon counts are Poisson, so the data term becomes Σ[(Ax)_i − b_i log(Ax)_i]; the MAP/ADMM recipe still applies.
    • TV suits depth maps: sharp edges, no flying pixels (11.67 m and 13.33 m invented by averaging vs. clean plateaus with TV), at a small contrast loss; slanted planes call for TGV.
    • Next: other imaging systems built on the same objective (§28).
    Part 8 · Compressive Imaging Elsewhere
    28

    CT, MRI and Hyperspectral Imaging

    Slides 113–138 survey other inverse problems; all are "minimize ½‖b − A x‖² + λΨ(x)" with a different A.

    Computed tomography (CT, slides 129–131). An x-ray source and a sensor rotate around the patient. Each reading is the total absorption along one straight line through the body; a full set of readings at one angle is a projection. The Fourier slice theorem links projections to the image: the 1D Fourier transform of the projection at angle θ equals the 2D Fourier transform of the image along a straight line through the origin at that same angle θ. So each angle fills in one line ("slice") of the image's 2D spectrum, and many angles fill the whole spectrum. Compressive CT uses fewer angles, so fewer slices, so less radiation dose and faster scans, with a prior filling in the gaps.

    Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI, slide 132). An MRI scanner measures the image's Fourier coefficients directly (radiologists call the frequency domain k-space). Compressive MRI measures fewer (often randomly chosen) coefficients, shortening scans, which matters for patients who must hold still. Here A = "Fourier transform, then keep only the measured frequencies."

    Hyperspectral imaging (slides 134–137). A hyperspectral image records many narrow wavelength bands per pixel (dozens to hundreds, instead of RGB's three): a 3D datacube (x, y, λ), here λ meaning wavelength. Conventional instruments scan, either over space (x, y) or over wavelength. CASSI (coded aperture snapshot spectral imager) captures the whole cube in one 2D photo: a coded aperture (a fixed random mask) patterns the light, then a disperser (a prism or grating, which bends each wavelength by a different amount) shifts each wavelength's copy sideways by a different distance, and all the shifted, masked copies land summed on one sensor. A = "mask, shift by wavelength, sum." Quality is moderate for a single snapshot, good with several coded shots (slide 137).

    A caution from medical imaging (slide 133). Practitioners are "often hesitant about priors": there are few guarantees of success; if reconstruction breaks it is not clear how; and "is that feature a reconstruction artifact or the thing I'm looking for?" A prior can hallucinate: produce plausible-looking detail that was never measured (a learned prior trained on healthy anatomy might smooth away a small tumor, or invent a structure).

    Same concept, different names

    CT = computed tomography = CAT scan. Fourier slice theorem = projection-slice theorem = central slice theorem. k-space = the frequency domain of an MRI image. Hyperspectral (many narrow bands) vs. multispectral (a handful of bands). Datacube = spectral cube. Disperser = prism or diffraction grating.

    Summary
    • CT: projections are slices of the 2D spectrum (Fourier slice theorem); compressive CT = fewer angles, less dose.
    • MRI measures Fourier coefficients directly; compressive MRI = fewer coefficients, faster scans.
    • Hyperspectral: CASSI codes and disperses a 3D (x, y, λ) cube onto one 2D sensor.
    • Rule to remember: every one of these is ½‖b − Ax‖² + λΨ(x) with its own A; priors help but can hallucinate.
    29

    Looking Ahead

    The lecture's closing notes (slide 139), restated with where each idea was built:

    • Compressive imaging is "an exploding area," and "most variants of compressive imaging problems can be implemented with ADMM" (§17–§26).
    • "Increasingly we want to learn the sensing matrices, reconstruction using neural networks and datasets": designing A (the patterns, masks, optics) jointly with the reconstruction, the learned-prior idea of §21 and the unrolling of §22 taken one step further.
    • The comparison on slide 98 (deconvolution at noise σ = 0.1) ranks the methods: Wiener clearly worst; Adam + TV and ADMM + TV close to each other; ADMM + DnCNN best.

    Where this goes next (optional). Later weeks apply the same "forward model + prior + solver" pattern to new kinds of measurements (light fields, neural representations); whenever a new camera appears, ask: what is A, what is Ψ, and which solver step handles each?

    Summary
    • One objective (½‖b − Ax‖² + λΨ(x)), two solvers (Adam: easy and general; ADMM: split, exact prox steps, faster convergence), many priors (TV, denoisers).
    • Rule to remember: for any new imaging problem, identify A (with Aᵀ), choose Ψ, and plug both into ADMM.
    Quick self-check

    Part 2. If asked why the data term is a squared error and where λ comes from, you should be able to answer using only "Gaussian noise," "−log," "Bayes' rule," and "prior."

    Part 3. If asked why TV keeps edges sharp but a squared-gradient penalty blurs them, use only "total climb," "ramp," and "ℓ₁." If asked why isotropic TV is "better," use only "same in every direction" and "diagonal edges."

    Part 4. If asked why Adam's learning rate is easier to choose than gradient descent's step size, use only "running average," "typical gradient size," and "scale."

    Part 5. If asked what each of ADMM's three steps does, use only "data prox," "prior prox," and "running sum of disagreements." If asked why the TV x-update for deconvolution needs no iterative solver but the single-pixel one does, use only "circulant," "Fourier domain," "division," and "conjugate gradient."

    Part 6. If asked why the least-norm reconstruction of a single-pixel camera looks like noise, use only "weighted sum of patterns," "null space," and "prior."

    Part 7. If asked how a single-pixel camera can measure depth, use only "time bin," "histogram," and "one single-pixel problem per bin." If asked why TV beats averaging on a depth map, use only "flying pixels" and "plateaus."

    Reference

    Running glossary

    Cumulative across the whole course, grouped by the week each term is actually covered (Week 1) or will be covered (later weeks) — so it doubles as a map of what's been learned and what's coming. One-sentence, beginner-level definitions.

    WEEK 1 Human visual system

    Aperture
    Camera terminology for the opening that controls how much light gets let in (a wider opening = more light); the pupil is the eye's own aperture. Deepened in Week 2.
    Image sensor
    The electronic chip behind a camera's lens that converts incoming light into a digital image, sitting where photographic film used to go; the retina plays the same biological role. Deepened in Week 2.
    Accommodation
    The eye changing focus by reshaping its lens via the ciliary muscle.
    Fovea
    The small, cone-dense pit in the retina responsible for sharp central vision.
    Rods / cones
    The retina's two photoreceptor types: rods for low-light/no-color vision, cones for color and fine detail.
    Metamerism
    Two physically different light spectra producing identical cone responses, so they look like the same color.
    Bayer color filter array / RGGB mosaic
    The physical grid of tiny red/green/green/blue filters glued onto a sensor, one per pixel, so each pixel measures only one color; the rest gets computationally filled in later (demosaicking, Week 3).
    Visual angle / arcminute
    The angular size an object subtends at the eye (1° = 60 arcmin); acuity and spatial frequency are both defined in these units, not raw distance.
    dpi (dots per inch)
    Pixel size flipped into pixel density: if a pixel is p inches wide, dpi = 1/p. Historically a printing term (ppi is the more precise word for screens), but used interchangeably with pixel density here (§9).
    Stereoscopic
    Literally "two-eyed viewing" (stereo + scopic); describes any device or display that feeds each eye a slightly different image (mimicking binocular disparity) so the brain perceives depth from an otherwise flat picture.
    Vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC)
    The mismatch, in stereo displays, between where the eyes converge (simulated depth) and where they must focus (actual screen distance).
    Stop
    A factor of 2 in light; stops = log₂(ratio), so +2 = 4× the light and −4 = 1/16. Camera exposure compensation ("+2 EV") is written in stops, usually in third-stop steps of 21/3 ≈ 1.26× (§14).
    Dynamic range
    The ratio between the brightest and darkest signal a system (eye, sensor, or display) can represent, in f-stops or orders of magnitude (§15).
    Spatial frequency
    How rapidly brightness varies across an image, in cycles per unit distance (or cycles per degree, perceptually); not to be confused with the frequency of light itself (color, §6) or temporal frequency (flicker/frame rate, §16.1). Full buildup, including why the same pattern's cycles-per-degree changes with viewing distance, in §16.
    Image frequency
    How rapidly brightness varies across a digital image's pixel grid (cycles per pixel), a fixed property of the file alone, independent of print size, display, or viewing distance. Converts into physical spatial frequency via dpi, and from there into cycles-per-degree via viewing distance — the full chain, worked numerically, is in §16.4.
    Weber contrast / Michelson contrast
    Two different formulas for "contrast": Weber for one feature against a uniform background, Michelson for a repeating pattern.
    Contrast Sensitivity Function (CSF)
    The curve describing how sensitive the eye is to a given spatial frequency; band-pass, peaking around 4–6 cycles per degree.
    Fourier transform (1D → 2D)
    The operation that rewrites a signal (a 1D signal like sound, or a 2D signal like an image) as a sum of sine waves of different frequency, amplitude, and phase; for images, the "wave" is a 2D sinusoidal grating with a horizontal frequency u and vertical frequency v. Introduced early, in §19, because HW1's hybrid-images task depends on it; formalized fully in Week 5.
    Spatial domain / frequency domain
    Two equally complete descriptions of the same image: spatial domain indexes by pixel location (ordinary "what color is here"); frequency domain indexes by (u,v) spatial-frequency pair (how much of that stripe pattern is present). The Fourier transform converts between them; nothing is lost (§19).
    Spectrum (magnitude / phase)
    The Fourier transform's output, one complex number per (u,v) pair: magnitude = how strong that frequency is, phase = how it's shifted. Low (u,v) = coarse image content, high (u,v) = fine detail (§19.3).
    DC component
    The (u,v) = (0,0) entry of a spectrum: zero spatial frequency, equal to the image's overall average brightness (§19.4).
    fftshift / ifftshift
    Reorders a raw FFT output so the DC component moves from a corner to the center (fftshift), or undoes that reordering before an inverse transform (ifftshift) — needed because of how the discrete Fourier transform indexes negative frequencies (§19.4).
    Convolution
    The operation of sliding a small list/grid of weights (the kernel) across a signal or image, multiplying and summing at each position: equivalently, stamping a copy of the kernel, scaled by each input value, at every input position and adding the stamps. Blurring is convolution; (x*h)[n] = Σ h[m]·x[n−m] (§20).
    Kernel / filter / mask / template
    The small list or grid of weights h that convolution slides over the signal (a tap is one weight; the support is where it is nonzero). Optics call the blur kernel the PSF, signal processing calls it the impulse response. (A frequency-domain mask in §21 is a different object.) (§20)
    Impulse / delta; impulse response
    The signal that is a single 1 among zeros; what a system outputs for it (a copy of its kernel) is its impulse response. For a camera, a single point of light and the blob it forms (§20; PSF in Week 4 §18.1).
    Linear shift-invariant (LSI) system
    A system where scaling/adding inputs scales/adds outputs (linear) and shifting the input just shifts the output (shift-invariant). Every LSI system is a convolution with its impulse response, which is why one PSF can describe a whole camera's blur (§20).
    Boundary handling (padding); full / same / valid
    What to assume beyond the signal's edge when a kernel overhangs it (zeros, repeated edge, mirror, or wrap-around, which the DFT assumes), and which output positions to keep (§20).
    Cross-correlation / matched filter
    Convolution's near-twin that slides the kernel without reversing it; correlating with a known pulse shape is the best linear way to detect that pulse in noise (used in LiDAR/ToF receivers) but does not sharpen (§20, §23).
    Convolution theorem
    Multiplying two spectra in the frequency domain is mathematically identical to convolving (a sliding weighted average of) the corresponding signals in the spatial domain; the mechanism behind frequency-domain filtering (motivated in §20.7, applied in §21) and, later, the PSF and deconvolution (Weeks 5–6).
    Low-pass / high-pass filter
    Operations that keep only coarse/smooth content, or only fine detail/edges, respectively.
    Deconvolution (first look)
    The inverse problem of convolution: given the blurred result (and usually the kernel), recover the sharp original, in the simplest case by dividing the spectrum by the kernel's spectrum (the inverse filter). Non-blind = kernel known; blind = kernel also unknown. Hard because it is ill-posed: exact zeros in the kernel's spectrum destroy information and near-zeros amplify noise, so regularization (added assumptions, e.g. the Wiener filter in Week 5, priors in Week 6) is needed. Relevant to defocus/motion blur, coded imaging, and sharpening LiDAR range returns (§23).
    Ill-posed problem
    One whose solution does not exist, is not unique, or changes wildly with tiny changes in the data; deconvolution is the standard example (§23).
    System impulse response (LiDAR)
    The waveform a LiDAR records for one ideal reflector, set by the laser pulse's shape and the detector's timing response; the measured return is the true returns convolved with it (§23).
    Inner product (dot product)
    Multiply two vectors entry by entry and add up; a cone's response is the inner product of the sampled spectrum with that cone's sampled sensitivity curve, and each Fourier coefficient is the inner product of a signal with one sinusoid (§6, §19.1).
    Linear map / linear operator
    A function that preserves sums and scaling, f(a·x + b·y) = a·f(x) + b·f(y), so it can be written as a matrix; the eye's spectrum-to-(L, M, S) map, the Bayer mosaic, and convolution are all examples (§6, §7, §20.7).
    Change of basis
    Rewriting the same vector's coordinates relative to a different set of basis vectors, via an invertible matrix; the DFT is a change of basis from spikes to sinusoids, and color spaces (XYZ, RGB) are changes of basis for (L, M, S) (§6, §19.1).
    Null space
    Every input a matrix sends to zero, i.e. every change it cannot see; metamers differ by a null-space vector of the cone matrix, and the Bayer mosaic's null space is why demosaicking can't just invert it (§6, §7).
    Projection
    A linear map P with P² = P that keeps one subspace and discards the rest; a 0/1 frequency mask is a projection onto the kept sinusoids, and I − P onto the others (§21, §22.2).
    Circulant / Toeplitz matrix
    A matrix whose every row is the row above shifted by one (with wrap-around for circulant; constant along each diagonal for Toeplitz); the matrix form of convolution with a fixed kernel (§20.7, §21).
    Diagonalization / eigenbasis
    Choosing a basis of eigenvectors (vectors a matrix only scales) so the matrix becomes diagonal; the Fourier basis diagonalizes every circulant matrix, with the kernel's DFT as eigenvalues, which is the convolution theorem (§21).

    WEEK 2 Digital Photography I — ray optics, aperture, sensor

    Ray optics
    Modeling light as straight-line rays, ignoring wave effects — the assumption behind pinhole-camera geometry (HW1) and the thin lens model (§1, §5).
    Condition number
    Largest ÷ smallest singular value of a matrix: how much measurement errors can be amplified when inverting it; about 2.0 × 10⁶ for a toy bare sensor, exactly 1 for an ideal pinhole (§1).
    Pinhole camera / camera obscura
    A barrier with a single small opening that lets only one ray per scene point reach the sensor, forming an inverted, scaled image (§2).
    Focal length (f)
    The distance from a pinhole or lens to the plane where a sharp image forms; an intrinsic property fixed at manufacture, not something a photographer adjusts by moving anything (§2, §5.2).
    Homogeneous coordinates
    Appending a 1 to a point, (X, Y, Z, 1), so perspective projection becomes a linear matrix product followed by one division by depth; the pinhole's 3×4 camera matrix (§2).
    Rank
    The number of independent directions a matrix's output can span; the pinhole camera matrix has rank 3 (depth is lost), and a 4×4 Bayer patch's 16×48 selection matrix has rank 16 (§2, §14).
    Optimal pinhole diameter
    The pinhole size that minimizes total image blur by balancing geometric blur (grows with diameter d) against diffraction spread (shrinks with d): d = 2√(fλ), where f is the pinhole-to-image-plane distance and λ is the wavelength of light (§3.1).
    Refraction
    The bending of light at a boundary between two materials of different optical density; the mechanism a lens uses to redirect rays (§5).
    Object distance (S) vs. sensor distance (S′)
    S is how far the actual subject sits from the lens, a property of the scene; S′ is how far the lens sits from the sensor, a property of the setup, adjusted by the focus ring. The thin lens equation ties the two to the (intrinsic) focal length; "focusing" means physically changing S′ until it matches what the equation demands for the S you want sharp (§5.1–5.3–4.3).
    Thin lens model / Gaussian lens formula
    A simplified lens model (zero thickness) built on two assumptions (center rays pass straight through; parallel rays converge at the focal plane), giving the thin lens equation 1/S + 1/S′ = 1/f, derived from two similar-triangle ray relations (§5.1).
    Magnification (m)
    The ratio of image height to object height produced by a lens, m = (S′ − f)/f = S′/S (§5.1).
    Ray transfer (ABCD) matrix
    A 2×2 matrix acting on a ray's (height, angle): travel by L is [[1, L], [0, 1]], a thin lens is [[1, 0], [−1/f, 1]], and the thin lens equation is the condition that their product's top-right entry is 0 (§5.1).
    Aberrations (spherical, chromatic, oblique/coma/distortion)
    Systematic deviations from ideal thin-lens focusing, caused respectively by spherical (not hyperbolic) lens shapes, wavelength-dependent refraction (dispersion), and off-axis geometry (§6).
    Aperture
    The opening controlling how much light enters a lens or pinhole; analogous to the iris/pupil. Deepened here with the f-number/stops formalism (§8).
    Field of view (FOV)
    The angular extent of scene captured, set by focal length and sensor size; the camera analog of Week 1's eye FOV (§10).
    f-number
    Ratio of focal length to aperture diameter (N = f/D); smaller means more light and shallower depth of field (§8).
    Stop
    A change in light by a factor of 2×, the standard unit for spacing aperture (and exposure) settings; the same unit as Week 1's dynamic-range f-stops (§8).
    Exposure compensation / EV
    A camera dial offsetting the meter's pick by a number of stops (Week 1 §14, Week 4 §2.3); absolute exposure value also labels an aperture/shutter combination, whose aperture half is explained in Week 2 §8.
    Defocus / actual object distance (O)
    A scene point at actual distance O ≠ the currently-focused distance S has rays that converge before or after the sensor plane, landing as a blurred circle of confusion instead of a sharp point; never happens with an ideal pinhole (§9.1).
    Circle of confusion
    The blur disc a defocused point forms on the sensor, c = m·D·|O − S|/O, derived from two similar-triangle relations tying the aperture, the focused distance S, and the actual distance O (§9.2).
    Depth of field
    The range of actual object distances whose circle of confusion stays below an acceptable (pixel-set) threshold ε, DOF ≈ 2εS/(mD) — centered on the focused distance S, not a free "actual distance"; the range's exact edges are its near and far distances, Onear = S/(1+k) and Ofar = S/(1-k) with k = ε/(mD) (§10.1, §10.3).
    Pixel pitch
    The center-to-center spacing of sensor pixels, a length (sensor width ÷ pixel count across it, typically a few µm); converts a blur threshold stated in pixels into the length the circle-of-confusion and depth-of-field formulas need (§10.2).
    Hyperfocal distance (H)
    The focus distance that extends the far edge of the depth of field to infinity, H = f²/(Nc), where this c is the fixed acceptable-blur threshold, not the general circle-of-confusion variable (§11); focusing at H makes the near edge of the depth of field exactly H/2 (evaluating §10.3's near-distance formula at k=1).
    Diffraction limit / numerical aperture (NA)
    The smallest resolvable spot size set by diffraction alone (Abbe's formula, d ≈ λ/(2·NA) ≈ λN); trades off against depth of field via f-number (§3, §12).
    Bokeh
    The look of out-of-focus blur; a defocused point becomes a copy of the aperture's outline (disc, polygon, cat's-eye, donut), size c ≈ (f²/N)|1/S − 1/O|; smooth vs. busy depends on the disc's intensity profile (§13).
    Apodization
    Fading an aperture's transmission toward its rim so the blur disc has soft edges (smooth bokeh), at the cost of some light (§13.3).
    Portrait mode / computational bokeh
    A depth map plus per-pixel synthetic disc blur imitating the optical bokeh that a phone's tiny lens cannot produce (§13.4).
    Time of flight (ToF) / LiDAR
    Measuring distance as light's round-trip delay, d = c_light·Δt/2 (3 m ≈ 20 ns); gives phones a direct depth map for portrait mode (§13.4; Week 4 §5, §21.3).
    Sensor
    The chip converting incident light into an electrical signal — the camera's "retina" (§14).
    Photoelectric effect
    A photon striking a photodiode knocking loose an electron; the basic photon-to-signal conversion inside every pixel (§14).
    Quantum efficiency / fill factor
    The fraction of incoming photons actually converted to signal, and the fraction of a pixel's area that is light-sensitive, respectively (§14).
    Underdetermined system
    Fewer equations (measurements) than unknowns, so infinitely many solutions fit the data; the Bayer mosaic (16 measurements of 48 unknowns in a 4×4 patch) is one, resolved only by adding assumptions (§14).
    Selection matrix
    A matrix whose every row holds a single 1 and zeros elsewhere, picking out one entry of the input; the color filter array written as a matrix (§14).
    CCD / CMOS
    Two sensor architectures for converting and reading out pixel charge; CCD trades speed/cost for sensitivity/noise, CMOS the reverse (§15).
    Rolling shutter / global shutter
    Row-by-row vs. all-at-once pixel exposure timing; rolling shutter can produce motion/flicker banding (e.g. 120 Hz AC-light flicker) but can also be exploited as a fine-grained temporal sensor (§16).
    Bit depth
    The number of discrete digital levels a sensor's ADC can output (12–14 bits RAW vs. 8 bits JPEG), an additional cap on dynamic range beyond the physical noise floor (§17, §20).
    Noise
    The random deviation of a measured pixel value from its expected value (mean); like the jitter in repeated kitchen-scale readings of the same apple (§18.1).
    Variance / standard deviation (first definition)
    Variance σ² is the average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation σ is its square root, the typical wobble in the pixel's own units. Independent noise variances add (§18.1; derived in Week 4 §3).
    Independent (uncorrelated) noise
    One random draw tells you nothing about another (e.g. different frames' readouts); the condition under which variances add (§18.1).
    Electrons vs. digital numbers (DN)
    Noise is easiest to reason about in electrons; the ADC converts to integer DN with a conversion gain g (DN = g × electrons; σ scales by g, variance by g²) (§18.2).
    Gaussian noise
    Additive, signal-independent sensor noise from thermal/read/amplifier sources (§18).
    Shot noise / read noise
    Shot noise: fundamental, signal-dependent randomness in photon arrival counts (Poisson-distributed, standard deviation = √N). Read noise: added by the sensor's own readout electronics, signal-independent (§18).
    Poisson distribution
    The distribution of counts of randomly-timed independent events at a steady average rate (raindrops in a bucket, photon arrivals); its variance equals its mean (§18.4).
    Dark current / dark current noise
    Electrons freed by heat in the photodiode even with no light; mean rate D e⁻/pixel/s, Poisson-random so variance D·t; the mean can be subtracted with a dark frame, the randomness cannot (§18.3).
    Quantization noise
    Rounding error when the ADC maps a continuous voltage to integer digital numbers; uniform in ±½ step, variance Δ²/12 for step Δ (§18.5).
    Fixed-pattern noise
    Repeatable pixel-to-pixel offset/gain differences from manufacturing; the same in every shot, so it does not average down across frames (§18.3).
    Dark frame
    An exposure with the lens capped, used to measure and subtract dark current's mean and fixed-pattern offsets (§18.5).
    Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
    Mean signal divided by its standard deviation; combines shot noise, dark current, and read noise into one formula (§19).

    WEEK 3 Digital Photography II — color science, ISP, demosaicking, denoising

    Spectral sensitivity function (SSF)
    A sensor's (eye cone or camera pixel's) per-wavelength responsiveness; its response to incident light is the integral of the light's spectral power distribution weighted by this function, R = ∫Φ(λ)f(λ)dλ (§2).
    Retinal (tristimulus) color space / metamerism
    The 3D space of achievable (S,M,L) cone responses; monochromatic light traces a "lasso curve" confined to the positive octant, and varying its strength sweeps out a convex cone with a horseshoe-shaped cross-section. Metamers (Week 1 §6) are physically different spectra landing on the same interior point of this cone (§3).
    Conic hull / convex hull
    All non-negative combinations of a set of vectors (conic hull), or all non-negative combinations whose weights also sum to 1 (convex hull); the achievable-color cone is the conic hull of the lasso vectors, and a gamut triangle is the convex hull of three primary chromaticities (§3, §7).
    CIE color matching functions
    The weights of three fixed primaries needed to visually match each pure spectral color; some matches require a negative coefficient, recorded when a primary had to be added to the test side instead of the primary side (§4).
    Standard observer
    An idealized "average" viewer built by pooling color-matching data from a small panel of real observers; formally it is its three color matching functions, and every CIE number describes what this averaged viewer would report (§4).
    Luminous efficiency function V(λ)
    The eye's relative brightness sensitivity at each wavelength (peak normalized to 1, in the green); CIE XYZ's Y coordinate was defined so its matching function equals V(λ), which makes Y luminance (§5).
    CIE XYZ / CIE RGB
    Two equivalent tristimulus bases for color: CIE RGB uses physically realizable primaries but needs negative coordinates for some colors; CIE XYZ guarantees non-negative coordinates for every color but its "primaries" aren't physically realizable light. No basis can have both (§5).
    CIE xy chromaticity diagram
    A 2D projection of 3D CIE XYZ (x=X/(X+Y+Z), y=Y/(X+Y+Z)) that discards luminance and keeps only hue/saturation (§6).
    Color gamut
    The set of colors a device can reproduce; for any 3 real primaries this is exactly the triangle of their chromaticity coordinates (a convex combination of 3 points), e.g. the sRGB gamut. Points outside the triangle need a negative coordinate and are unreproducible by that primary set (§7–§8).
    Barycentric coordinates
    The weights expressing a point as a weighted average of a triangle's corners; all positive means inside (D65 white in sRGB: (0.2120, 0.3922, 0.3959)), any negative means outside (§7).
    Display P3
    A wide-gamut RGB standard used by many phone/laptop screens: the cinema DCI-P3 primaries paired with a D65 white; the same RGB numbers mean a different color in Display P3 than in sRGB (§8).
    Image signal processor (ISP) pipeline
    The stage sequence turning a RAW Bayer image into a finished photo: demosaicking → denoising → gamut mapping → gamma correction → compression, plus dead-pixel removal, dark-frame subtraction, lens correction, and sharpening (§9).
    Exif
    Capture metadata (exposure, aperture, ISO, timestamp, lens) stored alongside an image's pixel data (§9).
    Gamma correction / sRGB
    Encoding linear sensor intensity with a power-law-like curve so finite bit-depth code steps match perceived (not physical) brightness steps; PS2's simplified form is I→I1/2.2, while the sRGB standard uses an exact piecewise linear/power-law formula (threshold 0.0031308, exponent 1/2.4, constant α=0.055) (§10).
    Denoising
    Computationally removing sensor noise after capture; most methods specialize one weighted-average framework, i_denoised(x) = (1/normalizer)·Σw(x,x')·i_noisy(x'), differing only in how the weight w is defined (§12.1).
    PSNR / MSE
    Mean squared error (averaged over pixels and color channels) and its log-scale, max-value-normalized ratio, PSNR=10·log₁₀(max²/MSE); the metric HW2 uses to numerically compare demosaicking methods (§13).
    Identity matrix Id
    The matrix that leaves every vector unchanged (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere); written Id in the Week 3 notes so it never clashes with the image I (§13, §17).
    Demosaicking
    Reconstructing full color from a Bayer sensor where each pixel measured only one channel; naive per-channel averaging (§14.1) improves through chrominance low-pass filtering (§14.3) and edge-directed methods (§14.4) to Malvar-He-Cutler (§14.5).
    Optical low-pass filter (OLPF)
    A birefringent glass layer in front of a sensor that pre-blurs incoming light to soften Bayer-sampling aliasing, at the cost of resolution (§14.2).
    Y′CbCr
    A luma (Y′) + chrominance (Cb, Cr) color representation, related to RGB by a fixed matrix and offset; used to filter only chrominance during demosaicking (§14.3) and to subsample only chrominance in JPEG (§19), since human vision is far more sensitive to luminance sharpness.
    Affine map
    A linear map plus a constant shift, u = Mv + o; RGB → Y′CbCr is affine because of its (16, 128, 128) offset, and is undone by v = M⁻¹(u − o) (§14.3).
    Malvar-He-Cutler demosaicking
    A linear demosaicking filter that adds a gain times a same-location, cross-channel gradient (Laplacian) correction to the naive interpolation estimate; published gains α=1/2, β=5/8, γ=3/4 (§14.5).
    Bilateral filter (Tomasi & Manduchi, 1998)
    A denoising filter weighting by the product of a spatial Gaussian and an intensity-difference Gaussian, so it smooths noise within a region but not across an edge ("edge-aware smoothing") (§16.2).
    Non-local means (Buades, Coll & Morel, 2005)
    A denoising filter weighting by patch similarity rather than single-pixel intensity, searching a bounded window and exploiting image self-similarity regardless of spatial distance (§16.3).
    NLM filtering parameter h / normalizer Z(i)
    HW2's symbols for non-local means: h sets how different two patches may be before their weight collapses (h² = 2σ² in these notes' form), and Z(i) is the sum of the weights, dividing by which makes them a true weighted average (§16.3).
    BM3D
    A state-of-the-art (not HW2-required) denoising method: group similar patches into 3D blocks and collaboratively filter each block via a DCT transform, coefficient thresholding, and inverse transform (§16.5).
    Unsharp masking
    Sharpening by adding back an amplified detail layer: sharpened = I + k·(I − blur(I)), with strength k chosen by the user (§17).
    Detail layer
    I − blur(I): the high image-frequency part of an image (edges and texture) that a blur removed; near zero in smooth regions (§17).
    Halo artifact
    The bright/dark outline hugging a strong edge after sharpening, caused by overshoot and undershoot when the edge itself lands in the detail layer (e.g. with a Gaussian blur); an edge-preserving bilateral blur largely avoids it (§17).
    Gamut mapping
    Converting a camera's native color gamut to a standard gamut (typically sRGB) via a camera XYZ → CIE XYZ → sRGB chain (§18).
    Gamut clipping
    The simplest gamut-mapping strategy: clamp each linear RGB channel of an out-of-gamut color to [0, 1] independently; cheap, but shifts hue/brightness and flattens saturated gradations into one patch (§18).
    Gamut compression
    A smoother gamut-mapping strategy that moves out-of-gamut colors inward (e.g. desaturating toward a gray of the same luminance), often nudging nearby in-gamut colors too so shades stay distinguishable; one source of camera "modes" (§18).
    Chroma subsampling
    Storing the chroma channels (Cb, Cr) at lower spatial resolution than luma (Y′), e.g. JPEG's 4:2:2 and 4:2:0, because the eye resolves fine color detail far less well than fine brightness detail (§11, §19).
    JPEG / DCT
    The standard lossy image compression pipeline: RGB→Y′CbCr, chroma subsampling (4:4:4/4:2:2/4:2:0), 8×8-block discrete cosine transform, coefficient quantization, and entropy/run-length coding (§19).
    Orthonormal basis (DCT)
    A basis of unit-length, mutually perpendicular vectors, so the inverse change of basis is just the transpose; JPEG's 64 8×8 DCT cosine patterns form one (§19).
    RAW file / dcraw
    A camera's container for its nearly unprocessed sensor mosaic plus the metadata needed to interpret it (filter pattern, black/white levels, white-balance gains, color matrix); dcraw is the classic command-line decoder, and rawpy the Python wrapper around its successor library, LibRaw (§20).
    Black level / white level
    The fixed electronic offset a no-light pixel reads (subtracted first) and the saturated maximum (divided by, after subtraction) that together put RAW values on a [0, 1] linear scale (§20).
    White balance
    Per-channel gains that make a neutral gray object come out with R = G = B, removing the light source's color cast; a diagonal matrix acting on (R, G, B) (§20).
    Deconvolution (defined in Week 1 §23; this is the Week 3 echo)
    Computationally undoing a known blur; Week 3 only previews this with one example slide (blur sources: defocus, geometric distortion, spherical/chromatic aberration, coma) and no formula — full treatment, and the inverse-problem framing, is Week 5–6's subject.

    WEEK 4 Great ideas in computational photography

    Exposure
    total light collected per unit sensor area, H = E·t ∝ L·t/N², set by exposure time and aperture (and scene brightness); ISO scales the recorded image's brightness but does not change H (§2.1–2.2).
    Exposure time / shutter speed / shutter time
    three names for one setting: how long the shutter lets each pixel collect light (e.g. 1/500 s, 2 s, "bulb"); a "fast shutter speed" is a short exposure time (§2.1).
    Shutter
    the mechanical curtain or electronic reset/readout that starts and stops light collection (§2.1).
    Equivalent exposures / reciprocity
    (time, aperture) pairs with the same t/N² deliver the same exposure; they differ in motion blur and depth of field instead of brightness (§2.2–2.3).
    Exposure value (EV)
    EV = log₂(N²/t), a single number labeling a family of equivalent exposures; one EV = one stop (§2.3).
    Full-well capacity / saturation (clipping)
    the maximum charge a pixel can hold; overexposed pixels hit it and all read the same maximum, losing detail irrecoverably (§2.4).
    Underexposure / overexposure
    too little light (signal buried in the noise floor) vs. too much (highlights saturate); correct exposure fits the scene inside the sensor's dynamic range (§2.4).
    ISO
    a sensor gain setting, usually applied before the ADC, that amplifies signal (and noise) without collecting more light (§2.5).
    Variance / standard deviation
    the average squared deviation of a noisy value from its mean, and its square root (the typical size of the wobble); independent noise variances add, and averaging K independent frames divides the variance by K: the K comes from the K terms in the summed variance, and K² from squaring the 1/K scale factor (§3; first defined in Week 2 §18).
    Poisson sum rule
    Pois(λ₁) + Pois(λ₂) = Pois(λ₁ + λ₂): adding photon counts from separate frames is statistically the same as counting once over the combined light; a Poisson variable's mean and variance are both λ (§3).
    Motion blur
    streaking from scene or camera motion during the exposure; streak length = image-plane speed × exposure time; mathematically a convolution with a box kernel (§4.3, §23.1).
    Burst photography
    capturing many short exposures and merging them, avoiding blur at the cost of paying read noise once per frame (§4.5).
    Active vs. passive sensing / range gating
    a passive camera collects existing light; an active sensor (LiDAR, ToF camera) supplies its own; range gating opens the detector only during a nanosecond window when the laser echo can arrive, an ultra-short exposure that rejects ambient light (§5).
    Integration time (ToF)
    a time-of-flight camera's name for exposure time: longer gives less noisy depth but more motion artifacts and saturation (§5.4).
    Light metering
    measuring a scene's overall brightness so the camera can pick an exposure setting; conventionally assumes the frame averages to about 18% reflectance (the "key," the same mid-gray convention as Week 3 §10's gamma example; real meter calibration works out to roughly 12–18%), which is exactly why metering can be "fooled" by scenes far brighter or darker than 18% gray (snow, a coal pile) (§6).
    Neutral density (ND) filter
    darkened glass/film in front of the lens that attenuates all wavelengths roughly equally, reducing light reaching the sensor without shifting color; strength measured in optical density, OD = log₁₀(1/transmittance) (§8.1).
    Calibration
    measuring things whose true values you already know, recording what an instrument reports for each, and thereby learning the mapping from reading to truth (e.g. weighing known reference weights on a kitchen scale; a thermometer in ice water at 0 °C) (§9.1).
    Calibration target
    an object, scene or setup whose true physical values are known in advance, used as the reference an instrument's reading is compared against; for a camera: a grayscale step chart or ColorChecker (known reflectances), a light at known intensity, or an exposure-time sweep (known relative light by construction) (§9.1, §9.3).
    Radiometric calibration
    measuring, and then undoing, a camera's response curve (its mapping from true light amount to recorded pixel value, bent by saturation, a noise floor and the in-camera tone curve) so recorded pixel values become proportional to light before HDR merging (§9).
    Response curve (camera response function, CRF)
    the plot or function f taking true light amount (scene flux times exposure time) to the pixel value a camera writes out; its inverse f⁻¹ linearizes pixel values (§9.1, §11).
    Tone reproduction curve
    the nonlinear function f a camera silently applies to its raw linear sensor reading before producing a viewable image (e.g. JPEG); a good generic fallback is a power law with γ ≈ 1/2.2 (§9.1, §9.4).
    ColorChecker
    a standardized chart of patches with known reflectance; its bottom row of six neutral grays (reflectance about 90% down to about 3%, optical density 0.05 to 1.50, not evenly spaced in log-reflectance) is one target used to calibrate a camera's tone reproduction curve (§9.3).
    sRGB decoding
    undoing the standard sRGB display curve (divide the 8-bit code by 255, then apply a short linear segment near black and a roughly 2.2–2.4 power law elsewhere) to get linear values proportional to scene light (§9.5).
    Triangle (hat) weight
    Debevec's HDR merge weight w(z) = 1 − |2z − 1| = 2·min(z, 1 − z): zero for black and saturated values, weight 1 at mid-gray z = 0.5, the straight-line alternative to the Gaussian weight (§10.4).
    Weight image
    the per-pixel confidence weights of one exposure shown as a grayscale image (bright = trusted), used to check which exposure covers which part of the scene (§10.4).
    Machine epsilon (ε) in log
    a tiny constant (the smallest relative float spacing) added before taking a logarithm so zero-valued pixels do not produce −∞ or NaN in the HDR merge (§10.5).
    Camera response function (CRF)
    the curve a camera applies between scene light and stored pixel value (the f of §9.2, or its inverse by convention); estimated by a linear least-squares fit in the Debevec–Malik method that OpenCV implements (§9.2, §11).
    HDR file formats — .pfm, Radiance .hdr, OpenEXR
    floating-point image formats needed because merged HDR pixel values span many orders of magnitude and would clip in a fixed-integer format; .hdr's trick is a single 8-bit exponent shared across all three color channels, so a pixel takes 32 bits instead of the 96 bits of three 32-bit floats (§12.3).
    Light probe / environment map
    an HDR photograph of a mirrored chrome sphere placed in a scene, capturing the entire surrounding illumination in one image; used for image-based relighting of synthetic objects (§12.4).
    Tone
    the brightness level of a pixel or region on the dark-to-light scale (usually luminance); in music a tone is a position on a pitch scale, in an image a position on a brightness scale. Not the color cast sense of "warm tone" (§13.1).
    Tonal range
    the span of tones in an image, from its darkest to its brightest region (§13.1).
    Tone curve
    a function mapping input tone to output tone; the in-camera one is baked in at capture and undone by calibration (§9), whereas a tonemapping curve is applied by you after HDR merging (§13.1, §14).
    Tone mapping
    applying a tone curve (or more elaborate local operator) to fit an image's huge tonal range into the small one a display can show while keeping the look of contrast and detail (analogy: a long scroll onto a postcard); compressing an image's (HDR or LDR) intensity values into the narrower range an actual display can show; progresses from a naive per-channel curve through intensity-only (xyY), edge-aware, and gradient-domain variants to avoid color washout and halo artifacts in turn (§13–§15).
    Gamma tonemapper (s·I)^γ
    the simplest global tonemap: scale by s, raise to a power γ < 1 to lift shadows, clip to [0, 1] (§14.1).
    Global vs. local tonemapping
    a global operator maps each pixel by its own value alone; a local operator also uses the pixel's neighbors to preserve local contrast (§14.2).
    xyY
    a reparameterization of Week 3 §6's CIE xy chromaticity diagram that adds back a luminance axis Y; tonemapping compresses Y alone and leaves xy (chromaticity) untouched, which is what keeps color-aware tonemapping from washing out hue/saturation (§15).
    HDR imaging
    precisely, producing a radiometrically linear image free of over-/under-exposure artifacts, via some combination of a single well-exposed RAW capture, radiometric calibration (§9), and/or bracketing-and-merging multiple exposures (§8, §10); the lecture is explicit that this is distinct from tonemapping — HDR imaging compensates for sensor limitations, tonemapping for display limitations — even though consumer "HDR mode" workflows routinely run both together (§16).
    PSF (point spread function)
    the blob a single point of light forms after passing through an optical system (a disc for a finite pinhole, a circle of confusion for a defocused lens, an Airy pattern at the diffraction limit); for a shift-invariant system, the whole image is the convolution of the ideal sharp image with this kernel. The convolution it relies on is built from scratch in Week 1 §20. Introduced and defined in full here; Week 5 formalizes it further in the deconvolution/Wiener-filter context (§18.1).
    OTF (optical transfer function)
    the 2D Fourier transform of the PSF; reports, frequency by frequency, how much of each spatial frequency survives the imaging system. A PSF/OTF is broadband when its OTF has no exact zero crossings — equivalently, its convolution matrix has a trivial null space and is, in principle, fully invertible (§18.2, §19.3).
    Coded aperture
    replacing a camera's plain circular aperture stop (or its refractive optics) with a deliberately patterned mask or phase element, chosen so the resulting point spread function's Fourier transform has no exact-zero frequencies ("broadband"), preserving information a plain aperture's blur would destroy (§19).
    Extended depth of field (EDOF)
    an image sharp at every depth simultaneously, produced by deliberately blurring everything with a depth-invariant, broadband PSF (via focal sweep or wavefront coding) and then deconvolving with one shared kernel (§20).
    Wavefront coding
    altering a lens's refractive/diffractive optics (rather than attenuating light with a mask) so a point source's rays no longer converge to a sharp focus at any one plane, giving an approximately depth-invariant PSF with no moving parts (§20.2).
    Focal sweep
    physically moving the sensor or focal plane through a range of positions during one exposure so every scene depth ends up blurred by approximately the same time-integrated kernel, giving a depth-invariant PSF (§20.2–§20.3).
    Monocular depth estimation
    recovering per-pixel depth from a single ordinary 2D photograph, either from learned pictorial cues (relative size, occlusion, perspective) or from a coded aperture's depth-dependent PSF shape/orientation (§21). (No precise Wikipedia article covers this specific technique combination — left unlinked.)
    Flutter shutter
    flickering the shutter open/closed in a coded temporal pattern during one exposure, replacing the ordinary box blur kernel's zero-crossing sinc spectrum with a broadband (zero-free) spectrum, so the resulting motion blur becomes invertible (§23).
    Duty cycle
    the fraction of an exposure during which a shutter (here, a flutter shutter) is open; it sets how much light a coded exposure collects (§23.3).
    Parabolic sweep / motion-invariant photography
    moving the camera itself along a parabolic (constantly accelerating) trajectory during exposure so every scene object, regardless of its own velocity, ends up blurred by the same motion-invariant kernel, enabling one shared deconvolution kernel across a whole frame (§24). (No Wikipedia article exists for this specific technique — left unlinked.)

    WEEK 5 Sampling, linear systems, deconvolution

    The Fourier toolkit

    Temporal / spatial / image frequency
    how often something repeats per second (Hz), per millimeter (cycles/mm), or per stored pixel (cycles/pixel); the wavelength of light is a separate quantity (§1).
    Amplitude, frequency, phase
    a wave A·cos(2πξx + φ) has height A, ξ cycles per unit length (period 1/ξ) and sideways shift φ (§2.1).
    Complex number / magnitude / angle / conjugate
    a pair (a, b) drawn as an arrow; multiplying complex numbers multiplies lengths and adds angles; the conjugate mirrors the arrow (§2.2).
    Euler's formula
    e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ: a unit arrow at angle θ, so A·e^{jφ} stores an amplitude and a phase and e^{j2πξx} is a wave of frequency ξ (§2.3).
    Negative frequency
    the second, oppositely spinning arrow that pairs with +ξ to make a real cosine; not a physical thing (§2.3).
    Fourier transform
    f̂(ξ) = ∫ f(x) e^{−j2πξx} dx: how much of each wave a signal contains; the inverse adds the waves back and loses nothing (§3.1).
    Primal domain / Fourier domain / spectrum
    the slides' names for the original space-or-time description and the per-frequency description of the same signal; the spectrum is the set of Fourier coefficients (§3.1).
    DC component
    the zero-frequency coefficient, equal to the signal's average (times N for the DFT); the bright center of a spectrum picture (§3.2).
    Conjugate symmetry
    real signals satisfy F(−k) = F(k)*, so a real image's magnitude spectrum looks the same rotated 180° (§3.3).
    Magnitude vs. phase
    magnitude = how strong each grating is, phase = where its stripes sit; swapping phases between two photos swaps what you recognize, so phase carries the structure (§4).
    Convolution
    (x ∗ h)[n] = Σ h[m] x[n − m]: stamp a scaled copy of the kernel at every input point and add (§5.1).
    Kernel / impulse response
    the weights a convolution slides over the signal; what comes out when a single impulse goes in (for optics, the PSF) (§5.1).
    LSI system (linear shift-invariant)
    any system where outputs add and scale with inputs and the same rule applies everywhere; every such system is a convolution with its impulse response (§5.1).
    Convolution theorem
    F{x ∗ g} = F{x}·F{g}: convolving in one domain is multiplying in the other (§5.2).
    Circulant matrix / eigenvector
    a matrix whose rows are successive cyclic shifts of one row (the form a wrap-around convolution takes); every sampled wave is an eigenvector of it, with the kernel's spectrum as eigenvalue (§5.2).
    Dirac delta (impulse)
    zero everywhere except one point, with area 1; its Fourier transform is the constant 1 (§6.1).
    Rectangular function (rect, box) / sinc
    rect(x) = 1 for |x| < ½; its transform sinc(ξ) = sin(πξ)/(πξ) crosses exactly zero at every nonzero integer (§6.2).
    Triangular function (tent)
    rect ∗ rect; its transform is sinc² (§6.3).
    Gaussian function
    the bell curve; its transform is another Gaussian of width 1/(2πσ), with no ripples or negative values in either domain (§6.4).
    Dirac comb (impulse train)
    impulses spaced T apart; its transform is a comb spaced 1/T apart (§6.5).
    Scaling theorem
    stretching a signal by a squeezes its spectrum by a: wide in one domain is narrow in the other (§6.6). (Covered in the Fourier transform article's properties; no standalone article.)

    Sampling and the DFT

    Sampling / sampling rate f_s
    keeping values only every T (f_s = 1/T); in the Fourier domain it adds copies of the spectrum at every multiple of f_s (§7).
    Sample (noun) / to sample (verb)
    a sample is one measured value of a continuous signal at one position or instant (one pixel value, one audio reading, one LiDAR digitizer tick); to sample is to take such measurements, usually evenly spaced. A pixel value is a sample of the light after averaging over the pixel's area (§7.1).
    Sampling interval T
    the spacing between consecutive samples (§7.1). Same concept, different names: sampling interval = sampling period = sample spacing; on a sensor, the pixel pitch.
    Sampling rate f_s = 1/T
    samples per unit time or length (§7.1). Same concept, different names: sampling rate = sampling frequency = sample rate; samples per second (S/s, e.g. 1 GS/s) in LiDAR and electronics; dpi/ppi for displays and printers.
    Resampling
    computing samples on a new grid from samples you already have (resizing, rotating, warping an image) (§7.1).
    Subsampling
    the simplest downsampling: keep every D-th sample and discard the rest, with no filtering (I[::4, ::4]) (§7.1).
    Decimation
    downsampling by a whole-number factor D; in signal-processing usage it includes a low-pass filter before discarding samples (§7.1, §19).
    Interpolation
    estimating values between existing samples; how upsampling fills in new samples (§7.1).
    Oversampling / undersampling
    sampling faster / slower than the signal needs (the Nyquist rate); undersampling causes aliasing (§7.1, §8).
    “Sample” in the statistical sense
    picking a few items at random from a collection (e.g. SGD's random rows of A); unrelated to measuring a continuous signal at evenly spaced points (§7.1, §32). See Sampling (statistics).
    Selection matrix
    a matrix with one 1 per row that keeps some entries of a vector and drops the rest; subsampling, a Bayer mosaic and SGD's row choice are all one (§7, §32).
    Spectral copy / replica
    the whole spectrum curve redrawn around a multiple of the sampling rate; copy m is the original slid by m·f_s (§7.2–§7.3). Same concept, different names: spectral copy = replica = spectral image (signal-processing term, unrelated to photographs) = alias (once copies overlap, §8). Analogy: a 12-hour clock face repeating every 12 hours.
    Frequency axis vs. sampling rate
    a spectrum plot's horizontal axis is the frequency of the signal's own waves (image frequency in cycles/pixel, spatial in cycles/mm, or temporal in Hz); the sampling rate f_s is not an axis but the distance between copies, and f_s/2 the edge of the central band (§7.3).
    Fixed ruler vs. per-current-pixel ruler
    two ways to label the frequency axis when resampling: cycles/mm or per original pixel (spectrum unchanged by resampling; copy spacing and Nyquist edge move) versus cycles per current pixel (Nyquist always 0.5; spectrum looks stretched by D after downsampling, squeezed by D after zero-stuffing). Same picture, converted by a factor D (§7.3, §19).
    Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem
    sampling at f_s ≥ 2 f_max keeps the spectral copies apart, so a band-limited signal can be recovered exactly (§8.1).
    Nyquist rate
    the minimum sampling rate needed to avoid aliasing for a given highest frequency present: 2 f_max (§8.1).
    Nyquist frequency
    f_s/2, the highest frequency a given sampling rate can represent (§8.1).
    Band-limited
    containing no frequencies above some f_max (§8.1).
    Aliasing
    distortion from sampling below a signal's true frequency content (e.g. moiré): a frequency above f_s/2 shows up at |f − f_s·round(f/f_s)|; it cannot be undone after sampling (§8.2–§8.4).
    Anti-aliasing
    low-pass filtering before sampling so nothing above the new Nyquist frequency remains (§8.4, §19).
    Fourier series
    the discrete set of coefficients of a periodic signal; repeating in one domain ⇔ sampled in the other (§9).
    DFT / FFT
    converts an image from pixel-brightness representation to spatial-frequency representation; FFT is the efficient algorithm for computing it. The underlying idea (image as sum of 2D waves) was introduced early, in Week 1 §19, for the hybrid-images homework. Exact formula: x̂[k] = Σ x[n] e^{−j2πkn/N}, an orthogonal change of basis x̂ = F x with F⁻¹ = F^H/N, treating the N samples as one period of a repeating signal (§10). The FFT computes it in about N log₂ N operations instead of N² by recursively splitting even and odd samples (§11).
    DFT matrix
    the N×N matrix with entries e^{−j2πkn/N}; its rows are orthogonal sampled waves (§10.2).
    Circular convolution / zero-padding
    DFT-based convolution wraps around the ends; pad to at least N + K − 1 samples for ordinary convolution (§10.3).
    Butterfly / twiddle factor
    the FFT's combine step x̂[k] = E[k] ± e^{−j2πk/N}O[k], and the complex factor in it (§11).

    The lens and the sensor as filters

    PSF (point spread function)
    how a single point of light gets smeared by an imaging system; introduced and defined in full in Week 4 §18.1 (coded-aperture imaging). This week: the lens's blur kernel, caused by aberrations and diffraction, so that blurred = sharp ∗ PSF when the blur is shift-invariant (§12).
    Optical aberration
    a real lens's departure from ideal focusing: chromatic (colors focus differently), spherical (edge rays focus closer); coma and distortion vary across the frame and so are not shift-invariant (§12.2).
    Diffraction
    bending/spreading of light through small openings — limits how sharply any lens or pinhole can focus. Computed with Fourier transforms: aperture → coherent PSF → incoherent PSF → OTF (§13).
    Fraunhofer diffraction
    the far-field regime in which the light pattern behind an opening is the opening's Fourier transform (§13.1).
    Coherent vs. incoherent light
    coherent (laser) waves add by amplitude and can interfere; incoherent (ordinary) light adds by intensity (§13.1).
    Coherent / incoherent PSF
    the wave amplitude on the sensor (the aperture's Fourier transform) and the intensity a sensor records (its squared magnitude) (§13.2).
    Autocorrelation
    the overlap of a function with a shifted copy of itself, as a function of shift; the aperture's autocorrelation is the OTF (§13.2).
    Airy disk / Airy pattern
    the diffraction PSF of a circular aperture: a bright disc of radius 1.22 λN plus faint rings (§13.4–§13.5).
    Jinc / Bessel function of the first kind
    the 2D (circular) counterpart of the sinc, J₁(2πρ)/ρ, the Fourier transform of a disc (§13.4, §16.2). (No standalone Wikipedia article for "jinc".)
    Anisotropic blur
    blur that depends on direction, as from a square aperture; circular apertures avoid it (§13.4).
    Beam divergence (LiDAR)
    a laser beam's angular spread, at best θ ≈ 1.22 λ/D for exit aperture D; sets the spot size and angular resolution (§13.6). See Beam divergence.
    Speckle
    the grainy interference pattern coherent light makes on reflection from a rough surface (§13.6).
    OTF / MTF
    the PSF's Fourier transform (complex: contrast and shift per frequency) and its magnitude (contrast only); a lens's OTF falls to zero at the cutoff 1/(λN) (§13–§14).
    Optical low-pass filter
    any optical element (lens blur, or a dedicated plate) that removes high spatial frequencies before the sensor (§14, §21).
    Irradiance
    light power per unit area arriving at the sensor, W/m² (§15.1).
    Pixel pitch / fill factor
    center-to-center pixel spacing p; fraction of each pixel's area that collects light (§15.1).
    Detector footprint MTF
    |sin(πξw)/(πξw)|, the loss of contrast from each pixel averaging over its width w; zero at ξ = 1/w (§15.2).
    Sensor Nyquist frequency
    1/(2p) cycles/mm for pixel pitch p; finer detail aliases (§15.3).

    Filtering

    Low-pass / high-pass / band-pass filter
    keep low frequencies (broad shapes), high frequencies (edges), or a ring in between (§16–§17).
    Oriented band-pass filter
    keep two opposite wedges of a ring, i.e. edges of one orientation (§17.3).
    Ringing / Gibbs phenomenon
    echo bands beside edges caused by a hard frequency cutoff, whose kernel (sinc/jinc) has negative lobes (§16.2).
    psf2otf
    pads a small kernel to the image size, circularly shifts its center to index (0, 0), and FFTs it, giving the OTF array for Fourier-domain filtering (§16.4).
    Unsharp masking
    sharpen by adding back the detail layer: x ∗ (δ + c_highpass), c_highpass = δ − c_lowpass (§17.2; first in Week 3 §17).
    Fourier optics / 4f system
    a lens produces the Fourier transform of a coherently lit input one focal length away; lens–mask–lens filters images optically (§18).

    Aliasing in practice

    Downsampling
    resampling to fewer samples, e.g. keeping every D-th sample; must be preceded by a low-pass filter below 1/(2D) cycles/pixel (§7.1, §19). Same concept, different names: downsampling and subsampling are often used interchangeably; when it matters, subsampling = discard without filtering, downsampling or decimation = filter first.
    Upsampling
    inserting new samples between existing ones, followed by a low-pass (interpolation) filter; creates no new detail (§7.1, §19.2). Deepened in §19.3: insert D − 1 zeros between samples (zero-stuffing), then low-pass filter at the old Nyquist frequency with gain D; the filter is the interpolation kernel.
    Zero-stuffing
    step 1 of upsampling: place each measured value in every D-th slot of a finer grid and write 0 between (§19.3). Same concept, different names: zero-stuffing = zero insertion = zero-filling = expansion. It leaves the spectrum unchanged but widens the representable band by D, so D − 1 extra copies sit inside it.
    Imaging (spectral images)
    the extra spectral copies that zero-stuffing leaves inside the widened band; upsampling's counterpart of aliasing, removed by the interpolation filter (§19.3). Not related to photographs.
    Interpolation kernel
    the small row of weights h that fills in new samples after zero-stuffing: nearest [1,1], linear [½,1,½] (D = 2), bicubic, Lanczos, ideal sinc; its frequency response decides how much of the extra copies survives (§19.3).
    Wagon-wheel effect
    temporal aliasing that makes a spinning wheel on film appear slow, stopped or reversed (§20.1).
    Pulse repetition frequency / range ambiguity
    a pulsed LiDAR's pulse rate; echoes from beyond c/(2·PRF) are timed from the wrong pulse and reported too close (§20.2a).
    Phase wrapping (CW time-of-flight)
    a continuous-wave ToF sensor's measured phase repeats every 2π, so distances repeat every c/(2 f_mod) (§20.2b).
    Birefringence / optical anti-aliasing filter
    a crystal that splits a ray in two by polarization; two layers on a sensor split each point into four, blurring just enough to prevent aliasing (§21).
    Moiré pattern
    false large-scale stripes produced when fine repeating detail aliases (§19, §21).

    Deconvolution

    Deconvolution (non-blind / blind)
    recovering the sharp image from a blurred one when the kernel is known / unknown (§22.1).
    Inverse filter
    divide the blurred spectrum by the OTF: i_est = F⁻¹(F(b)/F(k)); fails because it amplifies noise as N/K where the OTF is small (§22).
    Noise model b = k ∗ i + n
    blurred measurement = kernel ∗ sharp image + zero-mean noise independent of the image (§22.2).
    Signal-to-noise ratio per frequency, SNR(ω)
    signal variance ÷ noise variance at one frequency; PS4's practical estimate is mean pixel value ÷ noise σ (§23).
    Wiener filter
    a statistically optimal deconvolution method that accounts for noise: K*/(|K|² + 1/SNR), the inverse filter times a damping factor |K|²/(|K|² + 1/SNR) that falls to 0 where noise dominates. It minimizes the expected squared error and equals Tikhonov-regularized least squares with λ = 1/SNR (§23–§24, §30).
    Expected value / independence
    the long-run average of a random quantity; independent quantities satisfy E[IN] = E[I]E[N] (§24.1).
    Well-posed / ill-posed problem
    a problem is ill-posed if its solution may not exist, may not be unique, or changes wildly with tiny data changes; deconvolution is ill-posed (§33).

    Linear systems

    Linear system b = Ax
    measurements = image-formation matrix × unknown image vector; ray optics is linear in intensity (§26).
    Rank / null space
    the number of independent directions a matrix preserves / the inputs it sends to zero, which no measurement can reveal (§27.1).
    Condition number
    largest ÷ smallest singular value; how much measurement error can be amplified in the solution (§27.2).
    Singular value decomposition (SVD)
    A = UΣVᵀ: rotate, stretch each direction by a singular value, rotate; for a circulant blur the singular values are |OTF| (§27.3).
    Overdetermined / underdetermined system
    more / fewer measurements than unknowns (tall / wide A) (§28).
    Convex objective
    bowl-shaped, with a single minimum and no false valleys (§28).
    Least squares / residual / ℓ₂ norm
    minimize ½‖b − Ax‖₂², the sum of squared prediction misses r = b − Ax; ‖r‖₂ = √(Σ r_i²) (§29.1).
    Gradient
    the vector of partial derivatives, pointing uphill; for least squares it is Aᵀ(Ax − b) (§29.2).
    Normal equations
    AᵀAx = Aᵀb: the residual is perpendicular to every column of A, so least squares is an orthogonal projection onto the column space (§29.2).
    Pseudoinverse A⁺
    V Σ⁺ Uᵀ, where Σ⁺ divides by each nonzero singular value and puts 0 where a singular value is 0; x̂ = VΣ⁺Uᵀb is the least-squares solution, the best substitute for A⁻¹ when A is not square or not invertible (§29.2). Same concept, different names: pseudoinverse = Moore–Penrose inverse.
    Tikhonov regularization (ridge)
    x = (AᵀA + λI)⁻¹Aᵀb, adding λ to every eigenvalue so the system is always solvable; λ → 0 gives the least-norm solution (§30).
    Least-norm solution
    among all exact solutions of an underdetermined system, the shortest one (no null-space component) (§30).
    Filter factors
    the per-singular-value weights s²/(s² + λ) by which regularization multiplies the plain inverse's 1/s, giving s/(s² + λ) in place of 1/s (§30).
    Gradient descent / step size (learning rate)
    repeat x ← x − α∇f(x); for least squares ∇f = Aᵀ(Ax − b), and α must stay below 2/μ_max (§31.1).
    Function handle
    passing "multiply by A" and "multiply by Aᵀ" as functions instead of storing the matrix (§26, §31.1).
    Adjoint (of a convolution)
    Aᵀ for a blur: convolution with the flipped kernel, or multiplication by F{c}* in the Fourier domain (§31.2). See Hermitian adjoint.
    Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) / batch size
    gradient steps computed from a random subset of B rows; the estimate is unbiased (right on average) (§32).
    Wall-clock time / warm-up
    real elapsed time between two clock readings (time.time(), time.perf_counter()); the first call to a library function is often slower (warm-up), so time several runs and report the median or minimum, with both routes doing the same work (§16.4, §32).
    L1 norm ‖v‖₁ = Σ|v_i|
    the sum of absolute values (§31.3). Same concept, different names: ℓ₁ norm = L1 norm = Manhattan norm = taxicab norm.
    Least absolute deviations (LAD)
    minimizing ‖Ax − b‖₁ (also L1 regression); resists outliers (fitting a constant gives a median, not a mean) (§31.3).
    Subderivative / subgradient / subdifferential
    at a corner, the slope of any line through the corner that stays below the graph (subderivative; subgradient in several variables), and the set of all such slopes (subdifferential); for |t| at t = 0 it is every value in [−1, 1], elsewhere the sign of t (§31.3).
    Subgradient descent
    gradient descent with a subgradient in place of the gradient; with a fixed step size it jitters near the minimum, so the step is often shrunk over iterations (e.g. α_k ∝ 1/√k) (§31.3).
    Bias of an estimator (unbiased)
    an estimate whose average equals the true value, here E[g(x)] = ∇f(x) (§32).

    WEEK 6 Regularized inverse problems with ADMM

    The problem, restated

    Inverse problem
    recovering an unknown true signal from indirect or corrupted measurements; in plain words, "working backwards from what the camera recorded to what the scene was." This week every inverse problem takes one form, minimize ½‖b − Ax‖₂² + λΨ(x), with a different A for blur, a single-pixel camera, LiDAR, CT, MRI or hyperspectral imaging (§1, §10, §28).
    Ill-posed problem (restated)
    a question with no single trustworthy answer: many sharp images explain the same blurry photo, and dividing by small numbers amplifies noise; "there are infinitely many solutions that satisfy the measurements," so a prior is needed to pick one (§1–§2; built in Week 5 §22.1, §33).
    Circulant matrix (restated)
    the N×N matrix C a wrap-around blur becomes, each row the previous one shifted by one with the overflow coming back at the start; in plain words, "the image is treated as if printed on a loop." It is why C x ↔ F{c}·F{x}, Cᵀx ↔ F{c}*·F{x} and CᵀC x ↔ |F{c}|²·F{x} (§2).
    Solver
    a step-by-step search procedure that homes in on the best image; this week's two are Adam and ADMM (§1).

    Probability and the Bayesian view

    Random variable
    a quantity whose value is not fixed in advance but follows a pattern over many repetitions, like the noise in one pixel (§3).
    Probability density, p(·)
    how likely values near t are, per unit of t; in plain words, "a ranking of which values are likely." It can exceed 1; only the area under it over a range is a probability (§3).
    Gaussian (normal) density
    p(t) = 1/√(2πσ²)·exp(−(t − μ)²/(2σ²)), written t ∼ 𝒩(μ, σ²): a bell curve, "a pile of sand poured from one spot," with peak at the mean μ and width the standard deviation σ (σ² = the variance); its exponent is a squared distance, which is where squared errors come from (§3). Same concept, different names: Gaussian = normal = bell curve.
    Conditional density, p(b | x)
    "the density of b given x": how likely each measurement is if we assume the true image is x; the bar means "assuming" (§3).
    Independence → multiply
    quantities that do not influence each other (the noise in two different pixels) have a joint probability equal to the product of their separate ones, like two fair coins both landing heads, ½ × ½ (§3, §4).
    Proportional to (∝)
    p ∝ q means p = constant × q; constants never move a maximum or minimum, so they can be dropped (§3).
    Likelihood
    p(b | x) ∝ exp(−‖b − Ax‖₂²/(2σ²)) under Gaussian noise: a score of how well a candidate image explains the measured data; in plain words, "if this were the true scene, how believable is what we measured?" (§4). Same concept, different names: likelihood = image formation model in probabilistic form (slide 27) = data model = noise model.
    Bayes' rule
    p(x | b) = p(b | x)·p(x)/p(b): turns "given the image, how likely is this data?" into "given this data, how likely is each image?"; posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. In plain words, a doctor's diagnosis weighing how well symptoms fit (likelihood) against how common each illness is (prior) (§5). Same concept, different names: Bayes' rule = Bayes' theorem.
    Posterior
