    p(x | b), Latin for "coming after": how plausible image x is after seeing the data (§5).
    Prior
    p(x), "coming before": how plausible x is as an image before any data; real photos are likely, TV static is not (§5).
    Evidence
    p(b), how likely the data was overall, averaged over every possible image; the same for every candidate x, so it is a dropped constant (§5).
    MAP estimate
    x_MAP = argmin_x (1/(2σ²))‖b − Ax‖₂² + Ψ(x): the single image with the highest posterior, "the most likely image, after seeing the data," found by taking −log so products become sums (§5). Same concept, different names: MAP = maximum a posteriori = posterior mode (mode = the peak, the most common value).
    argmin
    "the value of x that makes the following expression smallest": the location of the minimum, not the minimum value itself (§5).
    Data fidelity term
    (1/(2σ²))‖b − Ax‖₂² (or ½‖b − Ax‖₂²), the part of the objective that comes from the noise and rewards reproducing the measurements; in plain words, "does the answer match what was measured?" (§4–§5). Same concept, different names: data fidelity term = data term = data-consistency term = loss (Week 5 §29) = −log likelihood.
    Natural image prior / regularization
    assumptions about what real images typically look like, used to make an ill-posed inverse problem solvable. Made precise this week as the regularizer Ψ(x) = −log p(x): a number that is small for plausible images, added to the data term as λΨ(x); in plain words, "a built-in sense of what a real photo should look like" (§5, §7). Same concept, different names: prior ↔ regularizer = regularization term = image prior = penalty, Ψ(x) (some slides write Γ(x)).
    Regularization weight λ
    the dial between "believe the data" (small λ) and "believe what images usually look like" (large λ); from the Bayesian derivation λ plays the role of σ² times the prior's strength, so more noise → larger λ (§5). A Gaussian prior gives Week 5's Tikhonov regularization, with λ = σ²/τ² (§5).

    Image priors

    Norm
    a rule that turns a list of numbers into one "size" that is never negative, is zero only for the all-zero list, doubles when every entry doubles, and obeys the triangle inequality (§6).
    ℓ₂ / ℓ₁ / "ℓ₀" norms
    straight-line length √(Σv_i²) (Euclidean); sum of absolute values Σ|v_i| (Manhattan / taxicab, "blocks walked on a grid"); number of nonzero entries (a counting "norm," not a true norm) (§6). Minimizing ℓ₁ gives sparse answers because the diamond-shaped ℓ₁ ball touches a line of solutions at a corner, where a coordinate is exactly zero; minimizing ℓ₂ spreads values out (§6).
    Sparse
    "thinly scattered": a vector whose entries are mostly exactly zero (small ℓ₀), a few meaningful values among zeros (§6).
    Laplace distribution
    p(t) ∝ exp(−|t|/β), the prior behind an ℓ₁ penalty: a sharper peak at 0 than a Gaussian and heavier tails; in plain words, "most values are exactly or nearly zero, but a few can be large," the statistics of image gradients (§6).
    Heavy tails
    tails are a curve's far-left and far-right ends (the large values); heavy tails fall off slowly, so large values stay reasonably likely rather than practically impossible as under a Gaussian (§6).
    Laplacian / curvature
    Δ, how much a pixel differs from the average of its neighbors, i.e. how much the brightness surface bends there; the kernel [0 1 0; 1 −4 1; 0 1 0], zero on flat regions and straight ramps. ‖Δx‖₂² is the "smooth everywhere" prior, good for blurry stuff, bad for photos with edges (§7). Same concept, different names: Laplacian = Laplace operator = Δ.
    Three example priors
    smooth images → ‖Δx‖₂ (slide 38; usually used squared, ‖Δx‖₂²); stars (mostly black) → ‖x‖₁; natural photos (flat regions separated by sharp edges) → TV(x), sparse image gradients (§7).
    Finite difference / image gradient
    "next pixel minus this pixel": (D_x x)[r, s] = x[r, s+1] − x[r, s] horizontally, (D_y x)[r, s] = x[r+1, s] − x[r, s] vertically, like measuring a staircase's slope one step at a time; each is a convolution with a 2-tap kernel, so in the Fourier domain D_x x = F⁻¹{F{d_x}·F{x}} (§8). Same concept, different names: finite difference = discrete derivative = image gradient (both directions stacked) = gradient operator D = grad_fn (HW5 Task 1–2) = opDx (HW5 Task 3). Not the objective gradient ∇f (§1, §11).
    Cross-correlation
    sliding a "multiply-and-sum template" across an image without flipping it; true convolution flips the kernel first, which is why the lecture's and PS5's d_x kernels look mirrored yet describe the same forward difference (§8).
    Gradient operator D = [D_x; D_y]
    the two difference images stacked: N pixels in, 2N numbers out; HW5 stores D x as an array of shape [2, M, N], horizontal in slot 0, vertical in slot 1 (§8).
    Circular (periodic) boundary
    the FFT's assumption that the image wraps around, so the last column's right-hand neighbor is the first column, "as if the image were printed on a tube"; it creates fake edges where opposite borders differ (§8).
    Dᵀ, the adjoint / divergence
    the transpose of the gradient operator, "send each difference back onto the two pixels it came from"; for the 1D forward difference with wrap-around, (Dᵀw)[i] = w[i−1] − w[i], and in the Fourier domain D_xᵀ ↔ F{d_x}* (§8). Same concept, different names: Dᵀ = opDtx = adjoint of the gradient = minus the discrete divergence ("how much a field of arrows spreads outward from a point, like water from a spring").
    DᵀD as a high-pass filter
    DᵀD is minus a Laplacian (1D kernel [−1, 2, −1]); in the Fourier domain |F{d_x}|² = 4 sin²(πk/N), 0 at k = 0 and largest (4) at the Nyquist frequency, so it "measures how much fine detail an image has" (§8).
    Total variation (TV)
    the sum over pixels of the image-gradient size, an ℓ₁-type penalty on image gradients; in plain words, a hike's total climb plus descent: one cliff and flat plains is cheap, constant small bumps (noise) are expensive. It charges a sharp step and a soft ramp the same, so edges survive and noise is removed (§7, §9). Same concept, different names: total variation = TV = TV regularizer = TV prior = TV pseudo-norm (= semi-norm).
    Isotropic TV
    Σ_i √((D_x x)_i² + (D_y x)_i²) = ‖D x‖₂,₁, the true length of each pixel's gradient arrow. "Isotropic" is Greek iso = "same" + tropos = "direction": behaves the same in every direction, like a round ball; it charges an edge the same whatever its orientation ("better," slide 41) (§9). Same concept, different names: isotropic TV = ℓ₂,₁ version ("ℓ₂ inside, ℓ₁ outside") = group sparsity (each pixel's two differences are kept or zeroed together).
    Anisotropic TV
    Σ_i (|(D_x x)_i| + |(D_y x)_i|) = ‖D_x x‖₁ + ‖D_y x‖₁, the gradient measured like a taxi on a grid. "Anisotropic" (an- = "not") means "direction matters," like wood that splits along the grain; it charges diagonal edges up to √2 ≈ 1.41× more and so reshapes them into stair-steps ("easier," slide 41, since each term uses one difference) (§9).
    Pseudo-norm / semi-norm
    "almost a norm": TV is zero for any constant image, not only the zero image, so it says nothing about overall brightness and the data term must pin that down (§9). Same concept, different names: pseudo-norm ("false norm") = semi-norm ("half norm").
    Staircasing
    TV's side effect of turning smooth slopes (a sky, a curved cheek) into flat terraces, "a ramp rebuilt as a staircase" (§9, §27.4).
    Chain rule
    the derivative of a function of a function is the product of the two derivatives (§9, §11).
    NaN / the torch.sqrt trap
    NaN = "not a number," what floating-point arithmetic returns for ∞ × 0; d/dt √t = 1/(2√t) is infinite at t = 0, so isotropic TV built with torch.sqrt gets a NaN gradient in flat regions, which poisons every pixel. Use torch.abs / torch.norm / torch.sum, which return a valid subgradient (0) at an exact zero (§9).

    Solver 1: Adam

    Objective
    the single number a solver tries to make as small as possible (§10–§11). Same concept, different names: objective = loss = cost.
    Objective gradient ∇f
    the vector of partial derivatives of the cost with respect to every unknown pixel value, "the direction in which the cost rises fastest"; what gradient descent and .backward() compute. Not the image gradient (§1, §11).
    Automatic differentiation / computational graph
    PyTorch records every operation of the loss computation in a computational graph ("a diagram of which numbers were combined, how, to make which"); loss.backward() walks it backwards with the chain rule and stores ∇f in x.grad; optim.zero_grad() clears it first because .backward() adds to what is stored (§11). Same concept, different names: automatic differentiation = autograd = backpropagation (in neural networks).
    PyTorch
    a Python library for numerical computing and neural networks that differentiates code automatically (§11).
    Adam
    a gradient method that keeps a running average of recent gradients (smoothing out jumps) and divides each pixel's step by a running estimate of its typical gradient size, so each pixel moves about α per step whatever the problem's scale; "convenient but doesn't always converge well," since it hovers near the minimum (§11). Same concept, different names: Adam = adaptive moment estimation.
    Moment (first / second)
    statistics word for an average of a power of a quantity: the 1st moment is the mean, the 2nd the mean of the square. In Adam, m_k (first moment) = running mean of gradients = momentum; v_k (second moment) = running mean of squared gradients, each pixel's typical gradient size (RMS after the square root) (§11).
    Momentum
    averaging gradients over steps so the consistent downhill direction builds up and back-and-forth flips cancel, "a ball rolling downhill does not stop at every bump" (§11).
    Exponential moving average
    a running average where each older value counts a fixed fraction (β) as much as the next newer one; β₁ = 0.9 remembers about 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10 steps, β₂ = 0.999 about 1000 (§11).
    Bias correction
    dividing Adam's running averages by 1 − β^k, which scales up the too-small early averages caused by starting m and v at 0 (at k = 1 it recovers g₁ exactly) (§11).
    Learning rate α (restated)
    roughly "how far a pixel value may move per step" in Adam; HW5 Task 1 uses 5 × 10⁻² (§11). Same concept, different names: learning rate = step size = α = lr.
    Hyperparameter
    a setting you choose before running (learning rate, λ, number of iterations), as opposed to the unknowns the solver finds (§11).

    Constrained optimization

    Splitting / split variable z
    giving the regularizer its own copy of the unknown, minimize f(x) + g(z) subject to Kx − z = 0 (K = D for TV, K = I for a denoiser prior); mathematically equivalent to the original, but lets each term be handled by the method it suits, like a plumber and an electrician each working on their own copy of a plan and meeting to reconcile (§13). Same concept, different names: split variable = slack variable (loosely) = auxiliary variable.
    Constraint
    a condition the answer is required to satisfy; "subject to" = "while obeying the condition that" (§13).
    Level curve
    a line of equal height of a function, like contour lines on a hiking map (§14). Same concept, different names: level curve = contour = isoline.
    Lagrange multiplier
    a number y attached to a constraint; at a constrained minimum the constraint is tangent to a level curve ("touches without crossing"), so ∇f is parallel to the constraint's gradient, ∇f = −y·∇(constraint). In plain words, finding the lowest point of a park while staying on a footpath (§14). Same concept, different names: Lagrange multiplier = dual variable = shadow price, written y on the slides (λ in many textbooks).
    Lagrangian
    L = f + yᵀ(constraint): one function whose zero partial derivatives give both the tangency condition and the constraint itself (§14).
    Shadow price
    what a constraint "costs" you: |y| is how much the best objective would improve if the constraint were loosened a little (§14).
    Primal / dual variables
    "primal" = the original unknowns (x, z); "dual" = the partners attached to the constraints (y, or u) (§14).
    Method of multipliers
    repeat: find the best x for the current price y, then raise the price in proportion to how much the constraint was broken, like a city raising a parking fine until nobody parks illegally (§15).
    Augmented Lagrangian
    L_ρ = f(x) + g(z) + yᵀ(Kx − z) + (ρ/2)‖Kx − z‖₂²: the Lagrangian plus a quadratic penalty ("augmented" = "with something added"); the penalty makes each sub-problem a well-behaved bowl, the multiplier makes the answer exact without ρ → ∞ (§15).
    Penalty parameter ρ
    how hard a constraint violation is punished in the augmented Lagrangian; you choose it (§15). A penalty alone (no multiplier) satisfies the constraint only as ρ → ∞ (§15, §22).
    Completing the square
    the school trick a r + (ρ/2)r² = (ρ/2)(r + a/ρ)² − a²/(2ρ), which merges the linear and quadratic constraint terms into one square (§16).
    Scaled dual variable u
    u = y/ρ, the price measured in the same units as Kx; gives the scaled form L_ρ = f(x) + g(z) + (ρ/2)‖Kx − z + u‖₂² − (ρ/2)‖u‖₂²; in ADMM it is the running total of past disagreements Kx − z, like a thermostat adding up how long the room has been too cold (§16–§17). Same concept, different names: u = scaled dual variable = scaled Lagrange multiplier = "running residual sum."

    Solver 2: ADMM and its steps

    ADMM
    an optimization algorithm splitting a hard joint problem into easier alternating sub-steps. Precisely: minimize the scaled augmented Lagrangian over x with z frozen (data step), over z with x frozen (prior step), then update the price u ← u + Kx − z; in plain words, "apply the data prox, apply the prior prox, update the price," repeated (HW5: 75 iterations) (§17). Same concept, different names: ADMM = alternating direction method of multipliers; x-update = data step; z-update = prior step = regularization step; u-update = dual update = dual ascent step.
    Proximal operator
    prox_{λf}(v) = argmin_x f(x) + (1/(2λ))‖x − v‖₂²: the point near v that does best on f, "a dog on a leash," where the dog wants f's lowest point and the leash ties it to v; both ADMM steps are proxes (§18). Same concept, different names: proximal operator = prox = proximal mapping = "proximal point of v with respect to f"; x-update = prox_{‖·‖₂,ρ}; z-update = prox_{‖·‖₁,ρ} (TV) or prox_{𝒟,ρ} (denoiser).
    Soft thresholding
    S_κ(v) = sign(v)·max(|v| − κ, 0) = max(1 − κ/|v|, 0)·v with κ = λ/ρ, the prox of the ℓ₁ norm: "shrink toward zero by κ, and stop at zero," like a tax with a flat deduction that wipes out anything smaller than κ; it is where TV's exact zeros (flat regions) come from (§19). Same concept, different names: soft thresholding = shrinkage = soft shrinkage = prox of the ℓ₁ norm, written 𝒮_κ. (No standalone Wikipedia article; covered under proximal operators.)
    Hard thresholding
    keep values above the threshold unchanged and set the rest to zero; unlike soft thresholding, it does not pull the survivors in by κ (§19).
    Block soft thresholding
    z_i = max(1 − κ/‖v_i‖₂, 0)·v_i: for isotropic TV, shrink each pixel's gradient arrow's length by κ, keep its direction, and zero it if it was shorter than κ (§19). Same concept, different names: block soft thresholding = group shrinkage = prox of the ℓ₂,₁ norm.
    Closed-form solution
    an answer written down directly, with no iterating, e.g. the deconvolution x-update (CᵀC + ρDᵀD)⁻¹(Cᵀb + ρDᵀv), computed by Fourier-domain division (§20). Same concept, different names: closed-form = analytic solution.
    Numerator / denominator (of the x-update)
    the denominator |F{c}|² + ρ(|F{d_x}|² + |F{d_y}|²) never changes during ADMM, so it is computed once; the numerator contains v = z − u and is recomputed every iteration ("nominator" in the HW text means numerator) (§20).

    Learned priors

    Denoiser 𝒟
    any method that removes noise from an image; the ADMM z-update argmin λΨ(z) + (ρ/2)‖v − z‖² is exactly MAP denoising of v with noise variance σ² = λ/ρ, so a denoiser can stand in for it (§21). Not the matrix D.
    Plug-and-play (PnP) prior
    using an off-the-shelf denoiser as ADMM's prior step, making the prior a replaceable part; there is no explicit Ψ and convex convergence guarantees no longer strictly apply, but it works well in practice (§21). Same concept, different names: plug-and-play prior = denoiser prior = learned prior (when the denoiser is a trained network) = "ADMM with denoiser."
    CNN
    a convolutional neural network: a stack of layers, each convolving the image with many small learned kernels and then applying a nonlinearity (§21).
    Nonlinearity
    a fixed bend applied between network layers, such as "replace negative values by 0"; without it a stack of convolutions would collapse into a single convolution (§21). Same concept, different names: nonlinearity = activation function.
    DnCNN
    "denoising convolutional neural network": HW5's 17-layer, 64-channel CNN trained on noise of standard deviation 25/255 ≈ 0.098, so λ/ρ is chosen to match that level (§21).
    Residual learning
    training a network to predict the noise and subtract it, because recognizing "what looks like noise" is easier than drawing a whole clean image (§21).
    Batch normalization
    a layer that rescales values using averages over the current training batch; model.eval() freezes it to its trained settings (§21).
    Non-local means (restated)
    a classical denoiser that averages pixels whose surrounding patches look alike; another possible plug-in for 𝒟 (§21; built in Week 3 §16.3).
    Half-quadratic splitting (HQS)
    ADMM without the price u: alternate x and z steps on f(x) + g(z) + (ρ/2)‖Dx − z‖₂²; simpler, but exact only as ρ → ∞, so "very sensitive to the penalty parameter" and usually run with a growing ρ (§22). Same concept, different names: HQS = half-quadratic splitting = quadratic penalty method with alternating minimization.
    Unrolled optimization
    running ADMM or HQS for a fixed K iterations, drawing the chain as layers of a network, and training per-iteration parameters (λ^(k), ρ^(k), even a separate denoiser) on example images; the idea behind the HW5 bonus (§22). Same concept, different names: unrolled optimization = algorithm unrolling = deep unfolding = "unrolled feedforward network."
    Feedforward network
    a pipeline of layers where data flows one way, each layer feeding the next, with no loops back (§22).
    Skip connection
    a shortcut that hands a layer's output directly to later layers, not only the next one ("DenseNet-like" names a well-known network built that way) (§22).
    Perceptual / adversarial loss
    perceptual: compare images by the features a trained network sees in them, closer to human judgment than pixel-by-pixel MSE; adversarial: a second network tries to tell results from real photos and the first is trained to fool it (§22).

    Compressive imaging and the single-pixel camera

    Single-pixel imaging
    reconstructing a full image from many single-value measurements plus known coded illumination patterns. Precisely: a lens images the scene onto a DMD, a pattern of mirrors sends part of the light to one photodiode, and each reading is b_m = a_mᵀx; repeat M times, b = Ax + η. Useful where large sensor arrays are expensive or impossible (infrared, terahertz) (§23).
    Digital micromirror device (DMD)
    a chip covered in hundreds of thousands of microscopic mirrors, each tilting "on" (toward the detector) or "off"; the on/off layout is the pattern (mask); the same chip is used in many video projectors (§23).
    Photodiode
    a one-pixel light meter that reports one number, the total light reaching it (§23).
    Measurement matrix A
    one pattern per row; for HW5 Task 3, M = 1024 random gray-level masks on a 64×64 (N = 4096) image; Afun = Ax (masks times image, summed), Atfun = Aᵀb (masks weighted by readings, summed) (§23). Same concept, different names: measurement matrix = sensing matrix = A. Watch the names: the starter code's N is the lecture's M.
    Compressive imaging
    measuring fewer numbers than pixels (M < N), so the camera "compresses while measuring" instead of measuring everything and compressing afterwards as JPEG does; the compression factor is N/M (HW5: 4) (§23). Same concept, different names: compressive imaging = compressed sensing setting (M < N).
    Under-determined (restated)
    more unknowns than equations, so infinitely many exact solutions exist (§23–§24; Week 5 §28). Same concept, different names: under-determined = compressive (M < N).
    Null space (restated)
    the changes to the image that leave every reading unchanged; any solution plus a null-space vector is another solution (§24; Week 5 §27.1).
    Least-norm solution
    x̃_ln = Aᵀ(AAᵀ)⁻¹b, the exact solution with the smallest ℓ₂ norm, derived with a Lagrange multiplier; it is a weighted sum of the patterns, contains no null-space part, and with random patterns looks like speckle ("not great," slide 112); Tikhonov in the limit λ → 0 (§24). Same concept, different names: least-norm = minimum-norm solution = "LN" = the pseudoinverse solution A⁺b for a wide A.
    Conjugate gradient (CG) method
    solves Ãw = b̃ for symmetric positive definite Ã using one matrix-vector product per step, by choosing conjugate directions that "never undo a previous step"; exact in at most N steps (§25). Used to compute least norm ((AAᵀ)w = b, then x = Aᵀw) and the single-pixel ADMM x-update (§24, §26). Same concept, different names: CG = conjugate gradient method.
    Conjugate (Ã-orthogonal) directions
    directions that would be perpendicular if space were stretched so the elliptical bowl became round; minimizing along one never spoils the minimization along the others (§25).
    Symmetric positive definite (SPD)
    Ã = Ãᵀ (mirror-image across the diagonal) and wᵀÃw > 0 for every nonzero w; in plain words, "a bowl that curves up in every direction," so it has exactly one lowest point. AAᵀ (independent patterns), AᵀA + ρDᵀD and AᵀA + ρI all qualify; semi-definite (≥ 0) also works if a solution exists (§25–§26). Same concept, different names: symmetric positive definite = SPD.
    Line search / steepest descent
    steepest descent is gradient descent with the best step length chosen each time ("go downhill until the ground starts rising"), an exact line search; on a stretched bowl it still zig-zags, which CG avoids (§25).
    Residual r_k (in CG)
    b̃ − Ãw_k, how far the current guess is from solving the system; also minus the bowl's objective gradient (§25).
    LinearOperator / matvec / matrix-free
    SciPy's wrapper that presents "a function that applies the matrix" (matvec = matrix-vector product) as a matrix to scipy.sparse.linalg.cg, which never stores the matrix; reshape to 64×64 before image functions and flatten after; cg returns (solution, info flag); its tolerance argument tol was renamed rtol in recent SciPy (§25). Same concept, different names: matrix-free = function handle (Week 5 §26) = LinearOperator.
    Linearly independent
    no pattern can be built as a weighted sum of the others; makes AAᵀ positive definite (§25).
    Warm start
    starting CG from the previous ADMM iteration's x (SciPy's x0) instead of zero, usually reaching the tolerance in fewer iterations; optional (§26).

    LiDAR

    LiDAR (restated)
    light detection and ranging: measures distance by timing laser light's round trip, d = ct/2 (§27; Week 4, Week 5 §20.2).
    Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD)
    a detector fast enough to time light to within a nanosecond that "clicks" on individual photons; expensive to build in large arrays, especially at infrared wavelengths like 1550 nm (§27.1).
    Scanning vs. flash vs. compressive LiDAR
    scanning: steer one beam point by point with one fast detector; flash: light the whole scene and use a full array of fast detectors; compressive (single-pixel): light the whole scene, apply DMD patterns, time the total return with one fast detector (§27.1). Same concept, different names: single-pixel LiDAR = compressive LiDAR = compressive depth imaging.
    Time bin / histogram
    the detector records counts of returned light in each short time slot (bin) after the pulse; a bin of width Δt is a depth slice Δd = cΔt/2 (0.15 m for 1 ns) (§27.2). Same concept, different names: time bin = histogram bin = range bin.
    Compressive LiDAR forward model B = AX
    each time bin is an ordinary single-pixel problem b_t = Ax_t sharing the same A; X's column t is the image of "what is at depth bin t," and each such slice is sparse (an ℓ₁ prior suits it) (§27.2).
    Multiplex advantage
    each pattern sends roughly half the scene's light to the detector instead of one pixel's worth, improving SNR when the detector's own electronic noise dominates (§27.2). Same concept, different names: multiplex advantage = Fellgett advantage (the spectroscopy name).
    Poisson distribution (restated)
    the probability law for counting independent random events, "raindrops landing on a tile in a minute"; photon counts follow it (shot noise, Week 2 §18), with standard deviation √mean, so a Gaussian noise model is wrong at low counts and the data term becomes Σ[(Ax)_i − b_i log(Ax)_i] (§27.3).
    Flying pixels
    invented depths that belong to no surface, points floating in mid-air between a foreground object and the background, produced at depth edges when foreground and background are mixed, either by the sensor itself (one pixel's light coming from both) or by ordinary averaging; TV smoothing does not add them (§27.4). Same concept, different names: flying pixels = mixed pixels = edge artifacts in depth maps.
    Contrast loss
    TV's small bias of moving each plateau toward its neighbor by λ ÷ (plateau length), because it charges for a jump's height (§27.4).
    Total generalized variation (TGV)
    a higher-order prior that penalizes changes in the gradient rather than the gradient itself, so a slanted plane costs nothing; fits depth maps of slanted surfaces better than plain TV (§9, §27.4).

    Compressive imaging elsewhere

    Computed tomography (CT)
    an x-ray source and sensor rotate around the patient, each reading the total absorption along one line; a full set of readings at one angle is a projection; compressive CT uses fewer angles for less dose (§28). Same concept, different names: CT = computed tomography = CAT scan.
    Fourier slice theorem
    the 1D Fourier transform of the projection at angle θ equals the 2D Fourier transform of the image along a line through the origin at that angle, so each angle fills in one "slice" of the spectrum (§28). Same concept, different names: Fourier slice theorem = projection-slice theorem = central slice theorem.
    MRI / k-space
    magnetic resonance imaging measures the image's Fourier coefficients directly; k-space is radiologists' name for that frequency domain; compressive MRI measures fewer coefficients for shorter scans, A = "Fourier transform, then keep the measured frequencies" (§28).
    Hyperspectral imaging / datacube
    recording many narrow wavelength bands per pixel (dozens to hundreds, vs. RGB's three), a 3D (x, y, λ) datacube with λ meaning wavelength (§28). Same concept, different names: datacube = spectral cube; hyperspectral (many narrow bands) vs. multispectral (a handful of bands).
    CASSI / coded aperture / disperser
    the coded aperture snapshot spectral imager captures the whole datacube in one 2D photo: a fixed random mask (coded aperture) patterns the light, a disperser (prism or grating, which bends each wavelength by a different amount) shifts each wavelength's copy sideways, and the sensor sums them; A = "mask, shift by wavelength, sum" (§28).
    Hallucination
    a prior producing plausible-looking detail that was never measured (e.g. a learned prior smoothing away a small tumor or inventing a structure); why medical practitioners are "often hesitant about priors" (§28).

    WEEK 9 Light field imaging

    Plenoptic function
    A theoretical function describing light intensity in every direction, at every point in space, wavelength and time — a photo is one small slice of it.
    Light field
    A practical capture of many directional rays (not just their per-pixel sum), often via camera arrays or microlens arrays.
    Light field / 3D display
    A display reproducing different images per viewing angle — one proposed fix for the vergence-accommodation conflict (Week 1 §13).

    WEEKS 10–12 Foundation models, neural rendering, black hole imaging

    Advanced / guest-lecture topics — brief pointers only, since detailed material isn't covered yet.

    Foundation model
    A large, general-purpose pretrained network (e.g. a diffusion model) adapted to imaging tasks like HDR generation or deblurring, rather than trained from scratch per task.
    Neural rendering
    Using neural networks, rather than a traditional graphics pipeline, to synthesize or reconstruct images/3D scenes from real photographs. (No dedicated Wikipedia article exists for this general term — left unlinked.)
